title: Win, Lose, Or Draw

jokes.text: In the event of an exact tie, the seat is awarded to the male candidate, and the female candidate is put in jail.
jokes.setup: A city commissioner is reading off official election procedures in a dry, bureaucratic manner.
jokes.punchline: The 'female candidate is put in jail' clause is delivered with the same flat officialness as the other rules.
jokes.explanation: The joke lands because of pure structural deadpan: a genuinely absurd and misogynistic old law is read with no editorial affect, as if it belongs alongside normal election rules. The specificity (not fired, not disqualified — JAIL) makes it funnier. It's a sharp satirical comment on how institutionalized sexism is often embedded in dusty old law, delivered with perfect economy and setting the satirical tone for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Election Commissioner
dialogue.line: According to city ordinance 47-B, women are only permitted to vote on Tuesdays and Thursdays, provided they have written permission from a male relative or employer.

jokes.text: Once again, I have to object. I don't think it would hold up in court but it is city law.
jokes.setup: The commissioner has just announced the absurd jail law.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's objection is strangely tepid — she's not outraged, just mildly noting it probably wouldn't survive legal scrutiny. The 'once again' implies she's raised this before.
jokes.explanation: 'Once again' is doing enormous work here — it implies this isn't new, that Leslie has fought this before and lost, and that she's resigned to flagging it weakly each time. The understatement of 'I don't think it would hold up in court' about an obviously unconstitutional law is perfectly Leslie: process-obsessed but ultimately deferential. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Election Commissioner
dialogue.line: Look, is it unconstitutional? Sure. But that's not really my department.

jokes.text: Watch what happens when I vote for Bobby Newport. [machine dispenses a candy bar]
jokes.setup: Bobby Newport is making his case about potentially rigged voting machines and demonstrates by voting for himself.
jokes.punchline: The machine literally dispenses a candy bar as a reward — blatant election bribery made childishly literal.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant visual gag — the candy bar is perfect because Sweetums is a candy company, so it's both a bribe AND a branded product. The absurdity of actual candy dispensing from a voting machine is exactly the right level of Pawnee stupidity. Strong character integration because only a Newport would install candy-dispensing voting machines.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me the voting machines might not be working right? But... but do they at least give out candy when you're done voting?

jokes.text: Shouldn't we be rewarding our citizens for voting? I'm never against anyone getting a candy bar.
jokes.setup: Bobby is confronted about the obviously corrupt voting machines dispensing candy.
jokes.punchline: His defense is not that it's not bribery — it's that candy is good and voting is good, so both together must be fine.
jokes.explanation: Peak Bobby Newport — his logic is not evil, just childlike. He genuinely cannot see what's wrong with giving people candy. 'I'm never against anyone getting a candy bar' is pure character comedy gold: it's not a calculated defense, it's his actual worldview. High character integration because this line could only come from Bobby.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Wait, why does it keep voting for me? That's... that's great!

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Bobby, the machine is broken.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Broken? It's working perfectly!

jokes.text: But watch what happens when you vote for me. [Leslie tries to demonstrate her machine, has to press it again, nothing impressive happens]
jokes.setup: Leslie wants to demonstrate her machine is superior/fair by contrast to the candy machine.
jokes.punchline: Her machine is broken or unhelpfully ordinary — she has to press it again, undercutting her righteous moment.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the deflation of Leslie's righteous setup. She's trying to make a principled point and the universe undercuts her. Works as a callback to joke #3 and as character comedy — Leslie's earnestness is always vulnerable to circumstance.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Random complaint about food that has nothing to do with the conversation

jokes.text: I'm sorry. I just don't see the problem.
jokes.setup: Leslie's machine has just failed to match the candy bar spectacle, and presumably officials are explaining the bribery problem.
jokes.punchline: Bobby's total sincerity — he genuinely cannot understand why candy bribery is bad.
jokes.explanation: Continues the Bobby Newport running gag of cheerful obtuseness. Short, economical, perfectly in character. Works as a capper to the candy machine bit.

jokes.text: I've only slept nine hours over the past four days. So, I'm right on the verge of a nervous breakdown.
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing the intense pressure of election day.
jokes.punchline: Nine hours over four days is objectively brutal sleep deprivation — but she frames it as being merely 'on the verge' of breakdown, not in one. The understatement is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Solid Leslie character beat — her obsessive work ethic expressed through sleep deprivation framed as somehow manageable. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We were going to do a sophisticated black-tie gala, but then we realized that Ben Wyatt is colorblind, so we changed it to a rave so he wouldn't notice if his outfit didn't match.

jokes.text: This isn't a bagel.
jokes.setup: Tom is apparently eating something he thought was a bagel while announcing the party.
jokes.punchline: The complete non-sequitur delivered mid-announcement — he's so sleep-deprived or distracted that he's eating something unidentified and only noticing now.
jokes.explanation: Three words doing massive comedic work. The joke is entirely in the non-sequitur — dropped in the middle of a completely unrelated announcement with zero explanation or follow-up. Perfect economy. The randomness earns its absurdism because it's so specifically mundane (not a bagel, not something exotic).

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I had this dream that I was at a beach resort, right? And it was super romantic. There were candles everywhere, soft music playing...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then somehow, inexplicably, Seal showed up. The singer. Just Seal, standing there in his leather outfit.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And I'm like, 'Seal? Why are you here? This is supposed to be romantic!' But he just kept singing 'Kiss From a Rose' over and over.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then David Blaine appeared and started doing magic tricks. Terrible magic tricks. Like, he kept trying to make the ocean disappear and it wasn't working.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And the whole time I'm supposed to be having this romantic moment with my future wife, but I'm just watching Seal and David Blaine argue about who's more relevant.

jokes.text: It is no longer a 'Pimps and Hoes' pajama party.
jokes.setup: Tom is announcing the election night party details.
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions the party's former theme — 'Pimps and Hoes' pajama party — as if this were a reasonable starting point that merely needed to be walked back.
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom Haverford character comedy — of course he planned a 'Pimps and Hoes' pajama party for election night. The funniest part is that he's the one announcing its cancellation, implying he agreed to drop it but still wanted credit for the original concept.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then this baby—this tiny baby—just hands me a briefcase with like ten million dollars in it. And I'm like, 'Thank you, baby.' And the baby's like, 'You're welcome, Tom. You deserve it.'

jokes.text: That idea was nixed by a certain uptight nerd who shall remain nameless.
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining why the party theme changed.
jokes.punchline: The 'who shall remain nameless' is obviously Leslie or Ben — the fake discretion while being completely transparent is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat for Tom. The 'shall remain nameless' fake discretion is a well-worn comedic device but executed with Tom's particular aggrieved flair. Not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: I'm going to vote for Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: I'm going to vote for her like a hundred times.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's not how voting works.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Oh, so you can only vote once per election?

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: That seems like a flaw in the system.

jokes.text: Last night, at approximately 2:30 a.m., I woke up from a dream that felt so real that it had to be a premonition. Me, Drake, and the T-Mobile girl were playing baccarat on a private jet. Ann Perkins walks up to me, and she says, 'Tommy, tomorrow night, I'm taking you back.'
jokes.setup: Tom is confidently explaining why he believes Ann will get back together with him tonight.
jokes.punchline: His 'premonition' involves Drake and the T-Mobile girl playing baccarat — the specific celebrity cameos in his dream are perfectly Tom-branded aspirational absurdism.
jokes.explanation: This is elite Tom Haverford character comedy. The dream details — Drake, specifically the T-Mobile girl, baccarat, a private jet — are not random; they're a perfect inventory of Tom's specific aspirational lifestyle brand. Every element earns its place. Ann's formal full-name address ('Tommy') and the clinical 'at approximately 2:30 a.m.' mock-serious framing make it even funnier. Justifiably above 8 — comparable in character specificity to the anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh sure, I'll take that job right after I'm drafted by the NBA.

jokes.text: Then, Blue Ivy Carter high-fived me and gave me $40 million.
jokes.setup: Tom has just finished describing his romantic dream premonition about Ann.
jokes.punchline: He casually appends that Blue Ivy Carter also appeared and gave him $40 million — a perfect escalation that makes clear the Ann part was actually the LESS absurd element.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. The escalation structure is perfect: Tom's dream already included Drake and the T-Mobile girl, but the punchline adds Blue Ivy Carter — an infant at this point in time — high-fiving him and handing over $40 million. The specificity of '$40 million' (not $10M, not 'a lot of money') and the sheer non-sequitur logic of an infant being a financial benefactor is inspired. It's a callback to #11 that retroactively makes the whole speech funnier. Comparable to the top anchor examples in escalation craft and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What is this thing?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Don't touch it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But I just want to see—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I said don't touch it, Andy.

jokes.text: Leslie, you can't vote for yourself, I don't think. I'm pretty sure that's illegal.
jokes.setup: Having revealed he's voting for Leslie, Bobby seems concerned about whether Leslie voting for herself is legal.
jokes.punchline: He has it completely backwards — voting for yourself is perfectly legal and voting for your opponent is the bizarre choice — but he's concerned about Leslie's (legal) self-vote.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant inversion: Bobby has voted for his opponent and is now worried that voting for yourself might be illegal. The 'I'm pretty sure' hedge makes it even better — he's not even confident in his wrong belief. Could only be Bobby Newport. The callback escalation here is perfectly constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, I need to tell you something. It was just a one-night stand.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Just one night?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, okay, it was two nights.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Two nights, Chris?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Fine, it was a weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: A weekend?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: A long weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: How long?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It's been three months.

jokes.text: Look. Your opponent is legendarily stupid, and I phoned it in pretty hard.
jokes.setup: Jen is complimenting Ben on his campaign management while offering him a job.
jokes.punchline: She qualifies the compliment by admitting she essentially tanked her own client's campaign through minimal effort — and that Ben's opponent being 'legendarily stupid' lowered the bar.
jokes.explanation: 'Legendarily stupid' is a great descriptor and 'I phoned it in pretty hard' is a wonderfully self-aware admission from a professional operative. Jen's brutal candor is the joke — the 'pretty hard' qualifier on 'phoned it in' is a lovely touch (she didn't just phone it in, she phoned it in HARD).

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, how many times did you two...?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: All in one night.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: All in one night?! I thought you meant over weeks!

jokes.text: Look at that. Look at that thing. What is that? Don't touch it.
jokes.setup: Ron has apparently encountered some object that disturbs or fascinates him at the party venue.
jokes.punchline: Ron's characteristic mixture of fascination and warning — 'Don't touch it' — implies something he finds either absurd or potentially dangerous.
jokes.explanation: Inferred visual gag — without seeing what Ron is reacting to, this is a moderate laugh built on Ron's character. The visual payoff would elevate it significantly on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Last night with Jen was incredible. It was like a perfect game of basketball - we had amazing chemistry, great timing, and I scored... multiple times.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, it was more like a triathlon. There were three distinct events, each with their own challenges and a brief transition period in between.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: And the stamina required? I've trained for marathons that were easier than last night. My heart rate was in the optimal cardio zone for a solid forty-five minutes.

jokes.text: Recently, in a moment of weakness, I had sex with Bobby Newport's campaign manager, Jennifer Barkley. Seriously? Yes, several times. And then, several more times. And then a couple more times. And then one more time.
jokes.setup: Chris approaches Ann asking for advice on a sensitive personal matter.
jokes.punchline: The escalating count of 'several times... several more times... a couple more times... one more time' is a perfect comedic escalation structure revealing a truly prolific one-night stand.
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure here is textbook-excellent. Each addition ('several more times... a couple more times... one more time') adds to the absurdity while the phrasing becomes progressively more sheepish. The 'moment of weakness' opener is undercut catastrophically by the sheer volume. Chris's earnest delivery makes it land even harder. This is above-8 quality escalation writing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April? April, where are you?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm under the table.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Why are you under the table?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Because I don't want to talk to anyone.

jokes.text: our ferocious sexual decathlon did radically improve my mood
jokes.setup: Chris is explaining his situation with Jen Barkley.
jokes.punchline: 'Ferocious sexual decathlon' is a characteristically Chris Traeger athletic framing for sex — making it sound like an Olympic event he trained for.
jokes.explanation: 'Ferocious sexual decathlon' is exceptional character writing. Chris's whole personality is athletic self-optimization and positive enthusiasm — applying the word 'decathlon' to sex is perfectly on-brand and unexpected. 'Radically improve my mood' as if it were a wellness intervention adds another layer. One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my god, I deleted all the files. All of them.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? How did you do that?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't know, I was trying to organize them and I just... they're gone.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, don't panic. We'll figure this out.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I am panicking!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to get under this table until this blows over.

jokes.text: Where are you? Under the table. Why are you hiding? Should I hide, too?
jokes.setup: Andy finds April in what appears to be hiding under a table in distress.
jokes.punchline: Andy's first instinct is not to ask what's wrong but whether HE should also hide — pure sweet-natured Andy logic.
jokes.explanation: 'Should I hide too?' is pure Andy — he doesn't assess the problem, he just wants to participate in whatever April is doing. Great character economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Have you tried turning it off and turning it back on again?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, that's not going to help. All the files are deleted.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, did you check if they're in the Recycle Bin? On my Xbox, everything goes to a recovery folder.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's... actually not terrible advice.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: See? Video games teach you real-world skills.

jokes.text: First of all, you did the right thing by hiding under this table.
jokes.setup: April has confessed to accidentally deleting all the Parks Department files.
jokes.punchline: Andy's reassurance begins not with 'we'll fix this' but with validating the choice to hide under a table as the correct first move.
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely excellent character comedy. Andy is trying to be supportive, and his idea of support is to first validate the hiding-under-a-table decision. It's perfectly Andy: well-meaning, wrong-headed, and somehow comforting. The 'First of all' structure implies there's a thoughtful list coming, which makes the absurd validation even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: I need help with this voting thing. How do I do it?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You just fill in the circle next to the candidate's name.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Okay, but which end of the pen do I use?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: The... the pointy end, Bobby.

dialogue.speaker: Bobby Newport
dialogue.line: Oh no, I already broke it.

jokes.text: I've been playing Xbox for years. I'm really good at fixing it when it freezes. I know exactly what to do.
jokes.setup: Andy promises to fix the government computer system that crashed and deleted all files.
jokes.punchline: His plan is based entirely on Xbox troubleshooting experience — transferring console gaming IT skills to a government data crisis.
jokes.explanation: Andy's confidence is the key — he doesn't say he'll try, he says he knows EXACTLY what to do. The Xbox-to-government-server tech transfer is absurd but totally within Andy's worldview where all frozen electronics are the same problem. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: News Anchor
dialogue.line: We're getting early returns on the city council race, and in a shocking turn of events, the porn star is winning.

jokes.text: One if you win, one if you lose. What if I tie? You need to write a tie speech for me. Something about the poetic nature of democracy, and how I'm going to fight this thing from my prison cell.
jokes.setup: Ben has prepared two speeches for all contingencies. Leslie asks about a tie.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's tie speech prompt includes directions for addressing the audience from prison — a callback to the opening jail-for-female-candidates law.
jokes.explanation: Beautiful callback to the opening gag. Leslie has clearly internalized the absurd jail law and is now planning around it. 'From my prison cell' delivered with total practicality is perfectly Leslie — she accepts this unjust reality and just wants to be rhetorically prepared for it. The callback structure rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. She's winning. We're losing to a porn star. This is... this is like if Italy had to choose between Michelangelo and Silvio Berlusconi, and they picked Berlusconi.

jokes.text: Hey, what's a good place to buy jeans?
jokes.setup: Leslie has just asked Ben what he was discussing with Jen Barkley, and Ben is clearly stalling.
jokes.punchline: His stalling deflection is asking about jeans — a completely random topic that signals he's buying time and is terrible at it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words that immediately tell us everything about Ben's panic and social awkwardness. The randomness of 'jeans' is funnier than any more sophisticated deflection would be. You have plenty of jeans' follow-up from Leslie shows she sees through it instantly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you are such a beautiful, articulate, well-spoken black woman.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm not black.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I am so sorry. You are such a beautiful, articulate, well-spoken woman of color.

jokes.text: You have plenty of jeans.
jokes.setup: Ben has attempted to deflect by asking about jeans.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response isn't 'what are you talking about' — it's the practical observation that he doesn't NEED jeans, cutting right through the deflection.
jokes.explanation: The response that reveals Leslie is not fooled, delivered with complete practicality. Three words that do everything needed.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I've been working on this campaign all day. I haven't stopped for a second.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Did you vote?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Vote? No, I've been too busy working on the campaign.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The campaign you were working on was to get people to vote.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And you didn't vote.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I didn't think about it.

jokes.text: I mean, it sounds amazing. But you know, six months in Washington, D.C. ... away from you.
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are trying to have a serious discussion about the Washington job offer.
jokes.punchline: The comedic beat is Ben's slow, pained trailing off — and the implied awkward pause — as he works his way around to saying he'd miss Leslie. The comedy is in his inability to just say the emotional thing directly.
jokes.explanation: A lighter comedic beat amid genuine emotion. The joke is mild — Ben's stammering avoidance of the actual feeling — but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If you can't vote, that's one less idiot voting. Now, if you could vote, that would be a disaster. So this is actually the best thing that could happen.

jokes.text: Yeah, we'll just talk about it. We'll mull it over. We'll look at it from every side, et cetera, et cetera. I'm going to go vote. Just fulfill a lifelong dream of mine and achieve one of my all-time happiest moments real quick. And then we will talk about it. Cool.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben agree to discuss the Washington job after the election.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'et cetera, et cetera' signals she's already emotionally checked out of THIS conversation, then she pivots to treating voting — her lifelong dream — as if it's a quick errand ('real quick') before getting back to the important matter.
jokes.explanation: Very Leslie — she's so excited to vote that she can't even finish the sentence about mulling things over, then frames 'fulfilling a lifelong dream' as a quick side errand. Good character integration with the 'Cool' mic-drop exit.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: So last night with Jen, I was thinking about efficiency. We tried seven different positions, and I calculated that missionary is actually the most effective for calorie burn per minute when you factor in the angle of core engagement.

jokes.text: Leslie, I can't figure this thing out. Can you help me? Yeah. Just hang on a second, Bobby. I got ink all over my hands, and the pen thingy came off the chain.
jokes.setup: Leslie is at the polls for her most important moment — voting for herself in her own election.
jokes.punchline: Bobby Newport, her opponent, cannot figure out the voting machine and asks HER for help — while she herself is struggling with basic pen mechanics.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is layered: Bobby asking his opponent for voting help is absurd on its face, and then we discover Leslie is also having trouble. 'The pen thingy came off the chain' is a perfect Leslie specificity — she knows everything about policy and government but in this moment the physical mechanics of voting are defeating her.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, it's going to be okay. You're not going to get fired.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You don't know that.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I do know that. And if you do get fired, we'll figure it out together. We could move to a new town, start over with new names.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We'll get fake IDs, live off the grid, maybe rob a few banks.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We'll become professional jewel thieves. We'll steal the Crown Jewels. We'll rob the Federal Reserve. We'll kidnap the president.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You need to stop.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We'll start our own country and declare war on the United States.

jokes.text: I don't get it. [Bobby Newport presumably still struggling with the ballot]
jokes.setup: Bobby has asked Leslie for help voting, she's given some basic instruction.
jokes.punchline: He still doesn't get it. The simplest civic act defeats him.
jokes.explanation: Short capper to the voting scene. 'I don't get it' as a ballot-filling response is the right amount of Bobby. Economy is good; concept is a bit easy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am absolutely exhausted. That was the most intense workout of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you've been in there for 22 seconds.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly. 22 seconds of pure cardio excellence.

jokes.text: With just 1% of the precincts reporting, adult film star, Brandi Maxxxx, has a commanding lead.
jokes.setup: Election results are starting to come in on the news.
jokes.punchline: The early leader with 1% reporting is the adult film actress who ran as a joke candidate — delivered with full news anchor gravitas.
jokes.explanation: The straight news delivery of 'commanding lead' for Brandi Maxxxx is the joke — treating a porn star's early polling numbers with the same serious treatment as a real candidate. A good Pawnee world-building gag.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't function with these boxing gloves still on.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. That's it. It's not Bobby Newport who's going to beat me. It's Brandi Maxxxx. The porn star. What is this, Italy?
jokes.setup: Leslie sees Brandi Maxxxx leading in early results.
jokes.punchline: 'What is this, Italy?' — Leslie's exasperated reference to Italy's history of electing celebrities/adult entertainers to office is both a sharp geopolitical joke and perfectly Leslie (she'd know this fact).
jokes.explanation: The Italy reference (Ilona Staller/Cicciolina, adult film actress who was elected to Italian parliament) is a surprisingly sophisticated joke that rewards knowledgeable viewers while also working as simple absurdist frustration. Leslie would absolutely know this fact. The delivery — 'The porn star. What is this, Italy?' — has excellent rhythm. One of the episode's sharper lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A gin and tonic? That's a drink for people who don't respect themselves or alcohol.

jokes.text: I've said this to you before, and I know it makes you uncomfortable. Oh, boy. But you're thoughtful and you're brilliant, and your ambiguous ethnic blend perfectly represents the dream of the American melting pot.
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to say something heartfelt to Ann to express gratitude.
jokes.punchline: 'Your ambiguous ethnic blend perfectly represents the dream of the American melting pot' — Leslie's compliment crosses from sincere into uncomfortably racially specific, and both characters know it ('I know it makes you uncomfortable').
jokes.explanation: This is a running gag within the series (Leslie regularly makes odd compliments to Ann about her appearance/ethnicity) executed at its finest. 'Ambiguous ethnic blend' is both cringe-inducing and genuinely Leslie — she means it as the highest compliment, she's cited it before, and she knows it's uncomfortable but can't stop herself. Perfect character integration. 'Oh, boy' from Ann before it even starts shows this is a well-worn bit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, I need some advice. Leslie wants me to change some things about myself.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. Absolutely not. Change is the enemy of progress.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But what if the changes would make me happier?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Happiness is irrelevant. You were born a certain way. You should die that way. The same clothes, the same breakfast, the same wood stain on your deck.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Even my clothes?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Especially your clothes. The moment you buy a new shirt, you've already lost. Next thing you know, you're eating different foods, living in a different house, voting for a different party. It's a slippery slope to chaos.

jokes.text: Ron? I handed out 1,000 leaflets today. That is a personal best. Now, I'm off to vote. The polls are closed.
jokes.setup: Jerry proudly reports his leaflet achievement to Ron while announcing he's going to vote.
jokes.punchline: The polls closed two hours ago. Jerry's personal best leafleting day was for nothing — he never voted.
jokes.explanation: The structure is beautifully constructed: Jerry's pride in his record leaflet distribution, combined with the word 'Now' suggesting perfect timing, gets demolished by the single word '6:00' from Ron. The irony is layered — Jerry worked hardest of all but didn't do the most basic thing. The callback at the very end ('Jerry forgot to vote / Damn it, Jerry!') makes this even better in retrospect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a list of things that will never change. My name will always be Ron Swanson. I will always love breakfast food. I will always make my own beef jerky. I will always oppose the government.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't own a cell phone. I don't use email. I don't have a bank account. I pay for everything in cash, which I keep buried on my property. I don't believe in Social Security. I have no driver's license.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I hunt my own food. I make my own clothes. I live completely outside of modern society, and frankly, I'm not sure why you people haven't figured that out yet.

jokes.text: Nothing you can do. Except hope Leslie doesn't lose by one vote.
jokes.setup: Jerry is distraught that he missed voting.
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'comfort' is to point out the one scenario where Jerry's failure would be catastrophic and irreversible.
jokes.explanation: This is Ron Swanson at his best — technically offering comfort while describing the worst possible outcome in exact, unhelpful detail. 'Nothing you can do' signals comfort, then 'except hope Leslie doesn't lose by one vote' is the twist. It's both funny and sets up legitimate stakes. The eventual 21-vote margin makes this a fantastic near-miss callback for rewatchers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe I lost.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: *laughs inappropriately*

jokes.text: and it's razor-thin. And getting razor-thinner.
jokes.setup: The news anchor is describing the election margins as results come in.
jokes.punchline: 'Razor-thinner' — not a real word, but spoken by the anchor with complete broadcast authority.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective Pawnee-media joke. The anchor uses an ungrammatical superlative with complete confidence. Good economy, moderate laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: Leslie, you need to concede. I can make this easy for you.

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: I'll give you a direct line to the President. Any time, day or night.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: The President of what?

dialogue.speaker: Jen Barkley
dialogue.line: The United States.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: Hey. What are you doing here? That was fun last night, you little screamer.
jokes.setup: Chris has sought out Jen at the party for a conversation.
jokes.punchline: Jen immediately and loudly references their sexual encounter with 'you little screamer' — a complete disregard for Chris's hope for a private conversation.
jokes.explanation: 'You little screamer' is both a funny revelation about Chris and a perfect Jen Barkley character moment — she's a power player who doesn't do discretion. The cringe comes from the public context. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, is that a real number? Because I could use that for fundraising.

jokes.text: There were moments that I didn't fully understand some of the physical shapes that we were making. But the sensations were amazing. So, I just went with it.
jokes.setup: Chris is responding to Jen's greeting and her description of their night.
jokes.punchline: 'The physical shapes that we were making' — Chris's athletic/anatomical framing of sex as geometric configurations he didn't fully comprehend is perfectly Chris.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. 'Physical shapes that we were making' is a remarkably original way to describe sex — clinical, geometric, yet somehow deeply earnest. It's Chris Traeger applied to intimacy: he approaches everything as a training exercise, so even baffling sex positions are filed under 'sensations were amazing, just went with it.' The character voice is so specific this line could only be Chris. Justifies the 8.5 rating.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm not even worried about the election anymore. I'm too busy tracking emerging lifestyle trends. Did you know that artisanal pickle water is going to be huge?

jokes.text: We're just getting supplies. Anybody need anything? Push pins, or... Okay, great.
jokes.setup: Chris and Jen are about to sneak into the supply room for a sexual encounter, but someone is watching.
jokes.punchline: Chris attempts to maintain the cover story ('getting supplies') while Jen clearly wants to move faster — the push pins improvisation while he pretends they have a legitimate errand is pure cringe comedy.
jokes.explanation: The 'push pins, or...' trailing off is a nice comedic beat — Chris scrambling for any office supply to name as cover. The awkwardness is well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is all my fault. I dragged all of you into this. You guys gave up everything - your jobs, your homes, your dignity - and for what? So I could chase some ridiculous dream?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm the worst friend in the entire world. I'm worse than Benedict Arnold. I'm worse than Genghis Khan. I'm worse than whoever invented the baby stroller that doesn't fit in the overhead compartment.

jokes.text: I'll tell you what, honey. Here's the deal. You get fired, I'll quit, and we'll leave together. I'm serious. Move to a new city, change our names, burn our fingertips off with acid, swap faces. What? If we have to.
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to comfort April about possibly getting fired for deleting the files.
jokes.punchline: His proposed solution escalates from 'move to a new city' to 'burn our fingertips off with acid' to 'swap faces' — each step further into absurdist action-movie territory while maintaining complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: This is the other contender for best joke in the episode, tied with joke #12. The escalation is perfectly structured: each step is funnier than the last, and crucially each step is delivered with complete sincerity and commitment. 'Burn our fingertips off with acid' is already extreme, and then 'swap faces' takes it to Face/Off movie territory. 'What? If we have to.' is the perfect button — Andy has anticipated April's objection and pre-justified it. This is what romantic absurdism looks like when it's done at the highest level. Andy's love expressed through action-movie solutions is the purest character expression in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've been drinking since I was a boy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, that's not something to be proud of.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not proud. I'm just stating facts.

jokes.text: Good. Yes. Nice. Keep punching. Did I hit your boob? Sorry. No. Great form. Maybe. I have no idea, actually. I don't know what I'm doing.
jokes.setup: Ann has arranged some stress-relief activity (boxing or a punching bag) for Leslie during the election wait.
jokes.punchline: The chaotic sequence reveals neither Ann nor Leslie knows what they're doing — Ann is coaching ('great form') while admitting she has no idea, and Leslie may have punched Ann in the breast.
jokes.explanation: A fun physical comedy sequence. 'Did I hit your boob?' is a funny specific, and Ann's coaching culminating in 'I have no idea, actually' is a good undermining of her earlier authority. Functional physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I want to be a forensic pathologist or a professional assassin. You know, something that really lets me combine my love of death with my love of money.

jokes.text: How long was that? Twenty-two seconds. Boy, that's disappointing.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been stress-boxing/exercising with Ann and asks how long she went.
jokes.punchline: Twenty-two seconds. Leslie's immediate 'Boy, that's disappointing' is hilariously resigned.
jokes.explanation: Good tight setup/punchline. 'Twenty-two seconds' is funny by itself, but 'Boy, that's disappointing' — with the 'Boy' doing heavy work — makes it a complete joke. Leslie's self-assessment is always funny when she applies it to physical limitations.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh my god, I deleted all the files! Everything is gone!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Relax. I prepared for Jerry's incompetence years ago with a secret backup system.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Of course you did.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I have backups of backups. Backups hidden in places Jerry will never find them. I even have a backup of my backup system.

jokes.text: Ann, I can't read it. Okay. Ann, my hands. Don't panic. Here. My hands, Ann. They're in these round gloves.
jokes.setup: Election results come in on Ann's phone during the boxing session.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has boxing gloves on and cannot read the phone or use her hands — her urgency completely thwarted by the round gloves she's wearing.
jokes.explanation: A good physical comedy payoff to the boxing setup — Leslie can't get election results because of her boxing gloves. 'They're in these round gloves' as a description is charmingly specific. The frenetic back-and-forth between Leslie's panic and Ann's calm is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, this is the most thoughtful gift anyone has ever given me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You like it? I thought you could use something to remember Washington by.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Remember Washington? Ben, look around my office. I have a Washington Monument on my desk, on my shelf, on my windowsill, in my drawer, on my wall...

jokes.text: Gin and tonic, please. Belay that order, Dana. Lagavulin, neat. Clear alcohols are for rich women on diets.
jokes.setup: Ben has ordered at the bar, stressed about the job offer.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately overrides Ben's order and dispenses his alcoholic philosophy — clear alcohols are for rich women on diets, therefore Lagavulin.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines and a peak Ron Swanson moment. 'Clear alcohols are for rich women on diets' is not just a joke — it's a complete worldview encapsulated in eight words. 'Belay that order, Dana' treats the bartender like a naval vessel crew, which is wonderfully Ron. This line has become genuinely iconic within Parks & Rec canon. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in sharpness and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We lost the recount. It's over. I can't believe this.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Actually, you won. By three votes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Ann, why would you do that to me?

jokes.text: Well, I've never been one for meeting new people or doing new things or eating new types of food or traveling outside of Southern Indiana. I've had the same haircut since 1978, and I've driven the same car since 1991. I've used the same wooden comb for three decades. I have one bowl. I still get my milk delivered by horse.
jokes.setup: Ben has asked Ron what he would do if faced with a choice between staying comfortable or pursuing a big opportunity.
jokes.punchline: Ron's answer is a perfectly escalating list of his own extreme conservatism culminating in 'I still get my milk delivered by horse' — which is so specific and anachronistic it becomes absurdist.
jokes.explanation: The escalation is brilliantly structured: each item in Ron's list of unchanging habits is slightly more extreme than the last. 'One bowl' is already wonderful minimalism, but 'I still get my milk delivered by horse' is a leap into anachronism that makes it absurdist. Then Ben's follow-up 'You do?' lands perfectly. This is Ron Swanson as a complete human philosophy expressed in ascending list form. Exceptional character integration — every word is Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I have some bad news about the election results.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, that's not possible. I was supposed to win!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Just kidding! You won! I was pranking you!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann! That's not funny!

jokes.text: You do? [Ben's follow-up to 'I still get my milk delivered by horse']
jokes.setup: Ron has just claimed he gets his milk delivered by horse.
jokes.punchline: Ben's simple 'You do?' confirms he's genuinely surprised and that Ron is completely serious — the understatement of the reaction is perfect.
jokes.explanation: The perfect straight-man reaction to the horse milk delivery. Two words that confirm the joke was landed. Economy of 10/10 — a lesser writer would over-explain it.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: So you got a job opening here? I'm looking for work.

dialogue.speaker: Parks Department Employee
dialogue.line: Well, we have an opening. Have you ever committed insurance fraud?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, tons of times. Why, is that bad?

jokes.text: But you and Leslie like to hold hands and jump off of cliffs together, into the great unknown. You two have a good relationship. I don't personally know what that's like, but I'm given to understand it means you're going to land on your feet.
jokes.setup: Ron has established his own life philosophy of extreme consistency. He now addresses Ben's actual situation.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't personally know what that's like' — Ron acknowledges his own relational limitations while genuinely encouraging Ben, which is funny because Ron admitting ignorance about a healthy relationship is both sad and funny.
jokes.explanation: This is warm Ron Swanson — advice-giving that acknowledges his own emotional limitations. The comedy is gentle: 'I don't personally know what that's like' is honest Ron, and 'I'm given to understand it means you're going to land on your feet' is Ron processing emotional wisdom through secondhand information. Beautifully in character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have a premonition that we're going to get back together.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, that's not a premonition, that's just wishful thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God, we're back together!

jokes.text: But if Leslie wins, you get my old job. Assistant City Manager, right? Seems that way. Then good luck, to the both of us.
jokes.setup: Ron has been giving Ben warm advice about relationships and opportunity.
jokes.punchline: Ron pivots to self-interest — he'll have to give up his job if Leslie wins, so he wishes them both luck, with the implication he's rooting for his own continued employment slightly more than Leslie's success.
jokes.explanation: A nice button to the Ron/Ben scene. 'Then good luck, to the both of us' has a perfectly Ron self-interested quality while not actually being mean. The 'to the both of us' implies his luck is equally at stake.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, I have to say, tonight was really something special. I mean, I showed up, I was present, I listened—well, I mostly thought about how well I was listening. And honestly, the way I handled that situation was probably the best anyone could have handled it. In fact, I'm pretty sure historians will study tonight as a turning point in human achievement. My achievement, specifically. I'm not trying to brag, but I may have just single-handedly improved the lives of everyone in this room by approximately 7%. Me. Just me. This is the best day of everyone's life and they don't even know it yet.

jokes.text: I have an update that contains new information.
jokes.setup: Someone bursts in with election news.
jokes.punchline: 'An update that contains new information' — an update by definition contains new information; this is bureaucratic tautology played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: A small Pawnee bureaucratic language joke. 'Contains new information' is a wonderfully redundant qualifier that fits the show's local government satire. Mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, you want to be a cop? All your dream jobs were cop jobs?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Huh. You know what? Maybe I should be a cop too.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Bobby Newport... scion of the Sweetums candy empire and amateur go-kart champion, has won the race.
jokes.setup: The news anchor is announcing the apparent winner of the City Council race.
jokes.punchline: 'Amateur go-kart champion' included in Bobby Newport's official biographical descriptor — in the gravest possible news-anchor tone.
jokes.explanation: 'Amateur go-kart champion' is the perfect absurd credential to include in a serious election broadcast. The word 'amateur' making it into the formal descriptor is a lovely touch — he's not even a professional go-kart champion.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We did it! We actually pulled off the whole thing!

dialogue.speaker: Everyone
dialogue.line: Cheers!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You know, if I hadn't accidentally deleted that email back in 2009, none of this would have happened.

jokes.text: Why are you laughing? Because my dream is dead.
jokes.setup: Upon hearing Bobby Newport has won, Leslie begins laughing.
jokes.punchline: 'Because my dream is dead.' — delivered with total calm as an explanation for the laughter, as if this is a perfectly rational response to catastrophic loss.
jokes.explanation: Dark and brilliant. The joke is in the complete calm with which Leslie explains her hysterical laughter — not 'I don't know why I'm laughing' but the precise and devastating 'Because my dream is dead.' It's the kind of thing you only say when you've gone past panic into a strange clarity. Perfect economy, deeply specific to Leslie's character. One of the episode's most quotable moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We did it! We actually did it!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And now we're gonna celebrate by going to the Sweetums factory and eating desserts until we die!

jokes.text: Oh, come on. It's over. Just concede. Newport won by 21 votes. That's well within the margin for a recount. Please don't do this. I really want to get out of here.
jokes.setup: Ben insists on a recount despite Jen's clear desire to leave.
jokes.punchline: Jen — a professional political operative — is arguing AGAINST exercising a legal right on behalf of her own candidate, because she wants to go home. Her exhaustion has completely overridden her professional instincts.
jokes.explanation: The irony of a campaign manager arguing against a recount is good character comedy. 'I really want to get out of here' is funny as the actual reason a professional gives for conceding.

jokes.text: How about this? Why don't I make you guys a deal? Okay, there's no deal in the world that we would ever possibly... I'll give you Joe Biden's home phone number. Now, hang on. That's interesting.
jokes.setup: Jen offers a deal to get Leslie to concede. Ben emphatically refuses before hearing it.
jokes.punchline: Joe Biden's home phone number. Ben's principled refusal immediately crumbles — 'Now, hang on. That's interesting.' The only thing that could penetrate Ben's integrity.
jokes.explanation: The setup is perfect: Ben's emphatic 'there's no deal in the world' makes his immediate backpedaling funnier. The specific currency — Joe Biden's HOME phone number, not office — is exactly right for this show's universe (Biden was VP in 2012, and his regular-guy appeal is the joke). Ben's 'That's interesting' rather than 'yes' shows he still has some dignity. Excellent structure.

jokes.text: Man, this is stressful. I picked the wrong week to do a juice cleanse.
jokes.setup: Everyone is stressed waiting for recount results.
jokes.punchline: Tom's stress is expressed through the irrelevant inconvenience of his juice cleanse timing — a deeply Tom prioritization of lifestyle concerns during a crisis.
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom — juice cleanse timing is his primary complaint during an election crisis. The specific wellness culture reference fits his character perfectly.

jokes.text: That's a nice chair. Corinthian leather. Solid mahogany frame with, what I believe, are hand-cut mortise and tenon joints. Pinned with oak. I was really looking forward to sitting in it.
jokes.setup: Ron has found Leslie alone in the commissioner's office, sitting in the chair she'd hoped to earn.
jokes.punchline: Ron's grief for Leslie is expressed entirely through woodworking and furniture appreciation — his emotional intelligence translated through craftsmanship evaluation.
jokes.explanation: This is beautifully written Ron. Rather than directly address Leslie's grief, he analyzes the chair with expert precision — and 'I was really looking forward to sitting in it' is devastating in its indirect way of saying he wanted her to win. The specificity of 'mortise and tenon joints, pinned with oak' is genuine woodworking knowledge deployed as emotional communication. Exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Let's go back to the party. You drive. I've had 11 whiskeys.
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered a heartfelt speech to Leslie about friendship and support.
jokes.punchline: The emotional moment is immediately deflated by Ron casually revealing he's had 11 whiskeys — stated not as an apology but as a practical reason Leslie should drive.
jokes.explanation: This is the perfect Ron Swanson button. After a surprisingly sincere and touching speech, he immediately undercuts it with a completely casual revelation — not three whiskeys, not five, but ELEVEN. Delivered not as an excuse or apology but as a logistics note. The number '11' is doing enormous comedic work. This is high-quotability, high-economy character comedy. Easily one of the episode's best lines and a legitimate 8+ moment.

jokes.text: Okay. That's good on places to live. Let's go back to dream jobs. If we have to start a new life, I have, 'Detective, F.B.I. agent, policeman, C.I.A. agent.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are doing a contingency planning exercise in case April is fired.
jokes.punchline: Andy's entire list of dream jobs for their new life consists exclusively of law enforcement/intelligence roles — revealing his career fantasy landscape with wonderful specificity.
jokes.explanation: The list being entirely law enforcement/spy jobs (and treating 'policeman' and 'detective' as different) is very Andy. The list has just enough variety to be funny — he clearly thinks these are very different careers.

jokes.text: A dental hygienist who's also a medium, so I can clean people's teeth and tell them when they're going to die.
jokes.setup: Andy has asked April what her dream job would be.
jokes.punchline: April's dream career combines two seemingly unrelated things — dental hygiene and telling people the date of their death — with the 'so I can' connecting them as if this is a perfectly logical combination.
jokes.explanation: This is the single most creative joke in the episode. The combination of dental hygiene (mundane, caring) with death prophecy (darkly April) is inspired. But what makes it exceptional is the 'so I can' construction — April presents this as a logical compound career, as if the reason to be a dental hygienist is to create the captive audience for announcing their death dates. It's perfectly April: dark, absurdist, specific, and delivered with complete sincerity. This approaches the Snip Snap anchor in originality and character specificity. Justifies a rare 9+ craft score.

jokes.text: That's brilliant.
jokes.setup: April has just described her dental hygienist/death medium dream job.
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate, sincere 'That's brilliant' — no hesitation, no confusion, complete acceptance and admiration.
jokes.explanation: Two words that tell us everything about Andy and April's relationship. He doesn't question it, he celebrates it. Good character integration as a reaction beat.

jokes.text: Let's make this fast. I almost made it with Councilman Howser before you interrupted us.
jokes.setup: Andy and April have gotten Donna to help fix the computer crisis.
jokes.punchline: Donna reveals she was in the middle of a romantic encounter with a councilman before being pulled away — delivered with complete calm as a logistical note.
jokes.explanation: Classic Donna — her romantic life is always more active and interesting than the plot, and she brings it up with perfect nonchalance. 'I almost made it' has a lovely schoolyard quality applied to adult romantic activity.

jokes.text: Jerry accidentally deletes things all the time. Ten years ago, I installed my own secret backup.
jokes.setup: The files seem lost. Donna calmly assesses the situation.
jokes.punchline: Donna has had a secret backup system running for TEN YEARS specifically because Jerry breaks things so often. This implies a decade of quiet, underappreciated problem-solving anticipating Jerry's failures.
jokes.explanation: Wonderful Jerry-adjacent joke that also reveals Donna's competence. The ten-year timeline is the kicker — she's been quietly protecting everyone from Jerry's incompetence for a decade without getting credit. It's a great piece of character and world-building simultaneously.

jokes.text: You have to go to Washington. I told you I'm turning it down. I was being selfish. You put your whole life on hold for me.
jokes.setup: Leslie opens a gift from Ben (a Washington Monument figurine) and reverses her earlier position on the job.
jokes.punchline: Leslie calling herself 'selfish' for wanting her long-term partner to stay with her is characteristically Leslie — her self-critique is always extreme.
jokes.explanation: Mild comedic beat within an emotional scene. Leslie calling wanting companionship 'selfish' is typical overachievement applied to relationships. Functional but not the episode's strongest.

jokes.text: I'll go visit you, then you come visit me, then I go visit you again, and then we make out in the Lincoln Bedroom and the Jefferson Memorial and the Supreme Court Gallery. We'll do it all over Washington.
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing how a long-distance relationship in Washington could work.
jokes.punchline: The list of romantic Washington locations escalates from the romantic (Lincoln Bedroom) to the increasingly public and inappropriate (Supreme Court Gallery) while maintaining her sincere enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Very Leslie — her romanticism and her government nerd-dom are perfectly fused. 'Supreme Court Gallery' as a make-out destination is peak Leslie Knope: civic reverence and romantic ambition in perfect collision.

jokes.text: Where did you get a Washington Monument figurine at midnight on a Tuesday? From my office. I have, like, 50 of them.
jokes.setup: Ben has just given Leslie a Washington Monument figurine as a gift encouraging him to take the D.C. job.
jokes.punchline: She has 50 of them in her office. Of course she does.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie characterization — of course she has 50 Washington Monument figurines in her office. Ben's slightly baffled 'Right.' acknowledges the absurdity while accepting it as completely normal for Leslie. Great economy.

jokes.text: That was really sneaky, Ann. I know. I couldn't resist.
jokes.setup: Ann delivered the recount results in a way that made Leslie think she had lost before revealing she actually won.
jokes.punchline: Ann's complete lack of apology — 'I couldn't resist' — is a lovely character moment. Even during Leslie's highest stakes moment, Ann engineered a troll.
jokes.explanation: Ann's 'I couldn't resist' after pranking her best friend with false bad news during her most important life moment is both endearing and funny. The friendship is so secure that this is fine.

jokes.text: You're kind of ruining it now.
jokes.setup: April has just loudly self-congratulated for not ruining the election during the victory celebration.
jokes.punchline: Someone points out that April's self-focused speech is, itself, ruining the moment she claims not to have ruined.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback button. The irony is exact: by celebrating not ruining things, April is ruining things. Five words, perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Great. That is great news. I'm going to see you in D.C. Yeah, I guess you will. Yeah. Damn it. I didn't get a chance to say goodbye to Chris. Oh, he's just right over there. He seems really busy. Anyway, would you tell him I said goodbye? Great. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Jen and Ann are having a brief exchange at the party.
jokes.punchline: Jen asks Ann — someone she's just met — to relay a goodbye to Chris rather than walking ten feet to say it herself. The lazy delegation is pure Jen.
jokes.explanation: Jen's casual delegation of a personal goodbye to a stranger because Chris is 'really busy' (he's right there) is great character economy. The 'Sorry we didn't get a chance to meet. I'm leaving.' is a nice button.

jokes.text: Sorry we didn't get a chance to meet. I'm Ann. That doesn't matter. I'm leaving.
jokes.setup: Ann tries to introduce herself to Jen.
jokes.punchline: 'That doesn't matter. I'm leaving.' — Jen's complete dismissal of Ann's identity is both rude and weirdly direct. She's not mean, just transactional.
jokes.explanation: 'That doesn't matter. I'm leaving.' is exceptional economy. It's not cruel — Jen just doesn't process social niceties. The bluntness is her character. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Was someone just talking about a job opening? Because guess who's got two thumbs and was just cleared from insurance fraud? This guy. You know? Got off on a technicality. What's the gig? I'm in.
jokes.setup: Ron has declined the Assistant City Manager job. Jean-Ralphio apparently overheard.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio immediately volunteers himself, citing his recent clearance from insurance fraud as a qualifier — 'Got off on a technicality' delivered as if this is a credential.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's brief appearance is perfectly executed. 'Two thumbs' + insurance fraud clearance + 'technicality' as a resume line is peak Jean-Ralphio: breezy confidence about genuinely disqualifying information. Only Jean-Ralphio would apply for a government position by referencing recent criminal clearance.

jokes.text: There's no job for you. That's a smart move. Go with your gut, right? I'll talk to you guys soon.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio has been told there's no job available.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio immediately reframes his rejection as the other person making a smart choice, then cheerfully departs as if it was all on his terms.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's complete inability to register rejection is a core character trait executed well here. 'That's a smart move' about not hiring him is both delusional and oddly charming.

jokes.text: Your victory speech, Councilwoman Knope. Someday, when I'm more emotionally stable, I want to read the concession speech you wrote for me. I never wrote it.
jokes.setup: Ben hands Leslie her victory speech. She asks to someday read the concession speech he prepared.
jokes.punchline: 'I never wrote it.' Ben never wrote the concession speech — he believed in her enough to not prepare for the loss.
jokes.explanation: Three words that are simultaneously a punchline and a deeply romantic statement. The comedy is in how Ben's earlier boast ('finished both of them last night') is revealed to have been only half true — and the half he skipped is the emotionally meaningful revelation. Beautiful structural economy.

jokes.text: Tommy! This party was amazing. You're amazing. You are ridiculous, but I like you. And I think that we should date all of it. Let's do it. Let's date. This is my dream! 'Nostratomus!' It's happening. Awesome.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ann appear to be getting back together at the party.
jokes.punchline: 'We should date all of it' — a Tom Haverford-ism that's grammatically strange but communicates his enthusiasm. 'Nostratomus!' as a victory cry is gloriously absurd. And his callback to his dream — 'This is my dream!' — referring to his premonition.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Tom's dream premonition pays off beautifully. 'Nostratomus!' as Tom's personal victory exclamation (a mangled Nostradamus) is inspired. 'Date all of it' is classic Tom Haverford language — excessive enthusiasm applied to a normal concept.

jokes.text: Hey, let's move in together. Totally. Really? Yeah. All right. No take-backs when we sober up, though, partner. No take-backs, partner. We're cowboys.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ann have just agreed to start dating.
jokes.punchline: Within minutes they've escalated to moving in together — and their mutual 'no take-backs' cowboy pact is a hilariously formal way to seal an impulsive drunk decision.
jokes.explanation: 'We're cowboys' as the logical conclusion to a no-take-backs drunk moving-in agreement is wonderfully Tom. The cowboy mythology applied to a mundane domestic decision is absurd escalation.

jokes.text: Great win. Great night. Great year. Hot wife. Jackpot.
jokes.setup: Chris is celebrating in his own way after the election victory.
jokes.punchline: Chris's list peaks at 'Jackpot' — his relentlessly positive cataloguing of blessings, delivered in his rapid-fire athletic way.
jokes.explanation: Very Chris — the staccato list of positives capped by 'Jackpot' is his character's essential optimism in list form. Economy is superb.

jokes.text: Good job, me.
jokes.setup: Chris is celebrating after the lists of positive things.
jokes.punchline: 'Good job, me.' — Chris self-congratulating with the same tone he'd use to praise an athlete, applied to himself.
jokes.explanation: Three words of pure character. 'Good job, me.' is Chris Traeger as a complete human philosophy — his relentless positivity turned on himself as a third-person recipient of his own coaching. Absolute economy. One of the most quotable moments in the episode for how much it captures in three words.

jokes.text: Almost everything you wrote on that board as a dream job was some type of police officer. How does this sound? 'Officer Dwyer, Pawnee P.D.'
jokes.setup: April has noticed that Andy's dream job list was all law enforcement variants and points this out as a revelation.
jokes.punchline: April suggests Andy become an actual police officer in Pawnee — and the way 'Officer Dwyer, Pawnee P.D.' is delivered implies Andy has never thought of this obvious solution to his obvious dream.
jokes.explanation: A season-arc setup disguised as a joke — Andy had been listing detective/cop/FBI fantasies without connecting them to an actual career path. April pointing this out as a discovery is sweet and funny. 'Officer Dwyer, Pawnee P.D.' has a lovely ring to it.

jokes.text: Guys, we're going to J.J.'s for victory waffles, and then we're staying up all night talking about our lives and our feelings. Non-negotiable. Let's go. City Council, bitches!
jokes.setup: Leslie is addressing her friends after winning.
jokes.punchline: 'City Council, bitches!' — Leslie's unprecedented profanity as a victory exclamation is both shocking and perfect, a joyful release from her usual decorum. 'Non-negotiable' applied to emotional vulnerability is also very Leslie.
jokes.explanation: This is the emotional and comedic peak of the episode. 'Non-negotiable' applied to staying up talking about feelings is wonderfully Leslie — coercive warmth. But 'City Council, bitches!' is what makes it exceptional: it's the only time Leslie swears in the episode (possibly the series to this point), and the contrast with her normal earnestness makes it a genuine crowd-pleaser. The joke is in the character violation that is somehow totally in character. Justifies a high impact score.

jokes.text: Jerry forgot to vote. Damn it, Jerry!
jokes.setup: The episode ends with a final title card or announcement revealing Jerry forgot to vote.
jokes.punchline: 'Damn it, Jerry!' — the callback to the running gag of Jerry's incompetence, but now with the specific devastating irony that he forgot to vote after spending the whole day campaigning for Leslie.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect episode tag. The setup was planted at 07:27 (Jerry misses the polls), paid off all episode by the 21-vote margin tension, and resolved here. 'Damn it, Jerry!' as a communal exclamation rewards everyone who remembered the planted detail. The 21-vote win makes the Jerry revelation hit especially hard in retrospect — had he voted, Leslie would have won by 22. This is textbook comedic structure across an entire episode. The brevity makes it even more devastating.

tmdb_overview: It's election day in Pawnee, and Leslie and Bobby Newport are separated by a razor-thin margin. While everyone waits with Leslie for the race to be called, they ponder their futures, and their new opportunities.
insight: Election night chaos sustains 87-point score through relentless character escalation over 48 jokes.
